parts.partTitle: Why SQL LIKE is Killing Your Database

beats.headline: Why does a leading wildcard kill your SQL performance?
beats.subline: It forces a full table scan. Here is how inverted indexes solve that.
beats.narration: A leading wildcard in SQL forces a full sequential scan across millions of rows. Elasticsearch avoids this by using an inverted index, mapping every term to a list of document IDs.

beats.title: Inverted Indexing Pipeline
beats.subtitle: From raw text to searchable postings lists
beats.narration: First, your documents pass through an analyzer. It breaks text into tokens, lowercases them, and stems words. Then, the inverted index maps these terms to a postings list of document IDs.

beats.title: The Anatomy of an Analyzer

steps.explanation: Cleans raw input, like stripping HTML tags before tokenization.
Exactly one: splits stream into tokens with position offsets.
Modifies tokens: stems, synonyms, or stop-word removal.

beats.narration: An analyzer is a three-stage pipeline. Character filters clean the input, the tokenizer splits it into chunks, and token filters normalize those chunks into searchable terms.

beats.title: Standard vs. Keyword Mapping
beats.narration: Use text fields for full-text search, but never aggregate on them—it causes heap pressure. Use keyword fields for exact filters, sorting, and faceted counts.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Inverted indexes map terms to doc IDs
Text is for search, Keyword is for facets
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): BM25 scoring & Lucene segments →
beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we explore BM25 relevance scoring and how Lucene segments keep search near-real-time.

beats.headline: Why does your search result rank higher than others?
beats.subline: It is not magic. It is BM25, the standard for modern relevance.
beats.narration: Why does one document appear at the top while another is buried? It is Okapi BM25, a scoring algorithm that balances term frequency and field length.

beats.title: BM25 Scoring Signals
beats.subtitle: The math behind relevance
beats.narration: BM25 uses three signals: IDF for rarity, TF saturation for diminishing returns on term repeats, and field length normalization to favor concise matches.

beats.title: Lucene Segment Lifecycle
beats.caption: Immutable segments ensure fast reads
beats.narration: Lucene segments are immutable. New data creates new segments, while deletes use a tombstone bitmap. Background merges periodically clean up these files to reclaim space.

beats.title: Avoid ?refresh=true

steps.explanation: Forcing refreshes creates tiny, fragmented segments that crush indexing speed.
Batch your writes to optimize throughput and segment merging.

beats.narration: Never force a refresh on every write. It creates tiny segments that destroy performance. Use the bulk API to batch your operations and let the background process handle indexing.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: BM25 balances rarity, frequency, and length

beats.narration: You now understand scoring and segments. In Part 3, we dive into Spring Data Elasticsearch and how to map fields for both search and aggregation.

beats.headline: Can you search and aggregate the same field?
beats.subline: Not if you map it wrong. Multi-fields are your best friend.
beats.narration: Trying to aggregate on a text field will crash your JVM with an OutOfMemoryError. The fix is using multi-fields to store the data in two different ways.

beats.title: The @MultiField Pattern

steps.explanation: Text type for full-text search and BM25 scoring.
Keyword type for exact filters, sorting, and aggregations.

beats.narration: Use the multi-field annotation. The main field handles full-text search, while the raw suffix uses the keyword type for exact filtering and faceted aggregations.

beats.title: Query vs Filter Context
beats.subtitle: Performance optimization
beats.narration: Separate your logic. Query context computes relevance scores, while filter context performs binary checks and uses cached bitsets for lightning-fast performance.

beats.title: NativeQuery Implementation
beats.code:
bool.must(m -> m.multiMatch(...)); // Scoring
bool.filter(f -> f.term(t -> t.field("inStock"))); // Cache

steps.explanation: Use for user-provided search terms that require scoring.
Use for structured data like status or price ranges.

beats.narration: Always put search terms in the must block to trigger scoring. Put structured filters like stock status in the filter block to take advantage of caching.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Use MultiField for search and facets
Query context scores, filter context caches
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Bulk indexing & error handling →
beats.narration: You are mastering the mapping. In Part 4, we tackle bulk indexing strategies and the critical importance of inspecting per-item errors.

beats.headline: Why is your bulk indexer returning 200 OK with failures?
beats.subline: Elasticsearch lies to you. Here is how to catch silent errors.
beats.narration: The bulk API returns 200 OK even if individual items fail. If you ignore the response errors, your search index will drift out of sync with your database.

beats.title: Inspecting Bulk Responses

steps.explanation: The bulk response is a collection; check the error flag explicitly.
Inspect every item for mapping or version conflicts.

beats.narration: Always check response errors. Even on a successful HTTP call, individual documents can fail due to mapping conflicts. Log these errors or push them to a dead-letter queue.

beats.title: Batching Strategy
beats.narration: Don't batch by count. Batch by size—aim for 5 to 15 megabytes per request. This keeps memory usage predictable and avoids overwhelming the coordinating node.

beats.title: Backfill Optimization
beats.subtitle: Before loading millions of docs
beats.narration: For large backfills, disable refreshes and replicas first. Load your data via bulk, then re-enable them. This drastically reduces the time required for massive indexing jobs.

beats.title: Part 4 Locked In
takeaways: Batch by size, not by count
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 5): CDC and Database Sync →
beats.narration: Bulk indexing is now your superpower. In Part 5, we finish by solving the biggest problem: keeping Elasticsearch in sync with your primary database using CDC.

beats.headline: Why do dual-writes always drift?
beats.subline: Because they lack atomicity. Here is the production-grade fix.
beats.narration: Dual-writes to Postgres and Elasticsearch are never atomic. You will eventually have ghost records or missing data. The only way to win is through Change Data Capture.

beats.title: CDC Architecture
beats.subtitle: Reliable data synchronization
beats.narration: Debezium tails the Postgres WAL, publishing changes to Kafka. An indexer consumer then processes these ordered events to update Elasticsearch. This ensures eventual consistency.

beats.title: Sync Approaches
beats.narration: Avoid dual-writes. Use CDC or a transactional outbox pattern. If Elasticsearch goes down, your database stays safe, and the consumer catches up once the cluster returns.

beats.title: Final Checklist
beats.caption: Production readiness
beats.narration: Follow this checklist: use multi-fields for facets, batch by size, always inspect bulk errors, and decouple your indexing with CDC. You are now ready for production search.
